L23@P1: Abstract
L24@P1: Endothelial cells initiate the inflammatory response by recruiting and activating leukocytes. IL-6 is not an agonist for
L25@P1: this, but we found soluble IL-6 receptor a-subunit (IL-6Ra),
L26@P1: with their constitutive IL-6 synthesis, stimulated endothelial cells to synthesize E-selectin, intracellular adhesion molecule-1, vascular cellular adhesion molecule-1, IL-6, and IL-8,
L27@P1: and to bind neutrophils. Neutrophils express significant
L28@P1: amounts of IL-6Ra and upon stimulation shed it: this material activates endothelial cells through a newly constituted
L29@P1: IL-6 receptor. Retrograde signaling from PMN activated in
L30@P1: the extravascular compartment to surrounding endothelial
L31@P1: cells will recruit more and a wider variety of leukocytes. The
L32@P1: limiting signal is a soluble receptor, not a cytokine. (J. Clin.
L33@P1: Invest. 1997. 100:2752–2756.) Key words: inflammation • leukocyte • E-selectin • interleukin-8 • chemokine
L34@P1: Introduction
L35@P1: Endothelium is the gatekeeper of the inflammatory response:
L36@P1: it attracts and activates leukocytes when endothelial cells are
L37@P1: appropriately stimulated (1). Marginated leukocytes rapidly
L38@P1: migrate to the extravascular space where exposure to additional stimuli causes release of reactive oxygen species and
L39@P1: proteolytic enzymes (2, 3). One consequence of the destructive
L40@P1: environment surrounding activated PMN is the shedding of
L41@P1: surface proteins such as L-selectin (4) and TNF receptors (5).
L42@P1: The functional consequence of this self-induced loss of surface
L43@P1: proteins is not clear as this occurs after migration into the extravascular compartment and full activation.
L44@P1: Neutrophils and monocytes express receptors for IL-6 consisting of a cytokine-binding alpha subunit (IL-6Ra)
L45@P1: 1
L46@P1:  and a homodimer of transmembrane, signaling gp130 subunits (6). Receptors for other members of the IL-6 family also contain the
L47@P1: signaling gp130 subunit and combinations of cytokine-specific
L48@P1: a-subunits and gp130-related subunits. Monocytes and COS-7
L49@P1: cells expressing recombinant IL-6Ra shed a portion of this receptor in response to the pleiotrophic agonist PMA in a form
L50@P1: able to bind cytokine and stimulate gp130 signaling (7, 8). IL-6
L51@P1: alone does not activate endothelial cells (although there is a
L52@P1: single report to the contrary [9]) even though oncostatin M, a
L53@P1: related family member whose receptor contains gp130 (10),
L54@P1: does activate the inflammatory response of these cells (11).
L55@P1: This result would be expected should endothelial cells lack
L56@P1: IL-6Ra. Since truncated, soluble IL-6Ra can confer IL-6 sensitivity to cells containing gp130 (12), including endothelial
L57@P1: cells (13), we determined whether a complex of IL-6 and
L58@P1: sIL-6Ra activated the inflammatory response of human endothelial cells. We found this complex did stimulate the inflammatory response. However, more striking was that the addition of sIL-6Ra alone activated endothelial cells: it appears
L59@P1: constitutive endothelial cell IL-6 expression was sufficient to
L60@P1: form an active complex with exogenous soluble receptor.
L61@P1: Endothelial cell activation depended on the concentration of
L62@P1: sIL-6Ra, showing the solublized receptor was the limiting
L63@P1: component of the signaling process. This observation is relevant as we found PMN exposed to the bacterial peptide FMLP
L64@P1: shed IL-6Ra in sufficient quantities to activate the inflammatory response of endothelial cells. These results suggest that
L65@P1: ablumenal neutrophil degranulation and cell surface protein
L66@P1: shedding could send a retrograde signal back through the endothelium to recruit more inflammatory cells from the circulation.

L120@P2: Results
L121@P2: sIL-6Ra activates endothelial cells to bind PMN. Oncostatin M,
L122@P2: but not its family member IL-6, activated endothelial cells to
L123@P2: bind quiescent PMN (Fig. 1 A). This shows that endothelial
L124@P2: cells possess functional gp130, which is common to both oncostatin M and IL-6 receptors (10), and suggests these cells lack
L125@P2: the IL-6Ra subunit of the IL-6 receptor that binds IL-6. We
L126@P2: analyzed surface IL-6Ra expression by flow cytometry and
L127@P2: mRNA levels by reverse transcriptase-PCR, which confirmed
L128@P2: that the insensitivity to IL-6 reflects a lack of this receptor
L129@P2: component (see Fig. 4 A). Consistent with this, we found that
L130@P2: addition of a complex of IL-6 and a truncated, soluble form of
L131@P2: the alpha subunit (sIL-6Ra) activated endothelial cell-dependent PMN adhesion (Fig. 1 A). Polymyxin B did not affect any
L132@P2: of these responses, so endotoxin was not responsible for this
L133@P2: stimulation. In a surprising result, we found that sIL-6Ra
L134@P2: alone was just as effective an agonist as the preformed complex of cytokine and its soluble receptor (Fig. 1 A). Moreover,
L135@P2: we found that PMN adhesion to the activated endothelial cells
L136@P2: was dependent on the concentration of sIL-6Ra (Fig. 1 B).
L137@P2: Thus the soluble receptor was the limiting component under
L138@P2: these conditions. PMN adhesion was an endothelial celldependent process as sIL-6Ra or IL-6 failed to stimulate PMN

L206@P4: a soluble form and still confer specific cytokine sensitivity (12,
L207@P4: 23). We found that soluble IL-6Ra recruited gp130 from the
L208@P4: very large (. 110,000 receptors per cell [24]) pool of endothelial cell oncostatin M receptors and allowed it to mimic proinflammatory effects of TNFa. An unexpected finding in this
L209@P4: regard was that sIL-6Ra did not require the addition of exogenous IL-6 to activate these cells. Endothelial cell-derived IL-6,
L210@P4: which is constitutively synthesized at low levels, was essential
L211@P4: for this activation, but the most significant aspect of this is that
L212@P4: the inflammatory response varied as a function of sIL-6a concentration. Thus the agonist to which primary, but not multiply
L213@P4: passed (22), endothelial cells respond in a graded fashion is
L214@P4: the soluble receptor, not the cytokine. Previously, the role of
L215@P4: sIL-6Ra has appeared to be mundane as its transgenic overexpression simply increases the half-life of IL-6 in the circulation
L216@P4: and sensitizes animals to an acute phase response (25). Our
L217@P4: data show that it can function as a true proinflammatory cytokine where its levels control endothelial cell function.
L218@P4: Inflammatory signaling is a vectoral process where stimulated endothelial cells recruit leukocytes from the circulation
L219@P4: to the extravascular compartment. To this end endothelial
L220@P4: cells synthesize and secrete several members of the C–X–C
L221@P4: and C–C class of chemokines that activate neutrophils and
L222@P4: monocytes, respectively. Few PMN products can reverse the
L223@P4: flow of information and activate endothelial cells: although
L224@P4: eventually cytokines synthesized by PMN (26) or massive free
L225@P4: radical production by activated PMN (27, 28) might do so.
L226@P4: Here we show that IL-6Ra is rapidly shed from FMLP-activated PMN in sufficient quantities to allow activated PMN to
L227@P4: efficiently stimulate endothelial cells. Proteolytic shedding of
L228@P4: external surface proteins after activation serves uncertain purposes (29), although modification of adhesion is clearly one
L229@P4: such function (4). The IL-6 receptor is shed from monocytes
L230@P4: stimulated with the potent tumor promoter PMA and, as we
L231@P4: show here, is shed from PMN after activation by a relevant,
L232@P4: pathophysiologic agonist, FMLP. The role of IL-6 receptors on
L233@P4: neutrophils has not been well defined, although it weakly induces platelet-activating factor synthesis (30) and weakly synergizes with TNF to enhance the respiratory burst (31). One
L234@P4: outcome of our data is that the target of IL-6 signaling is not
L235@P4: just the PMN expressing the IL-6 receptor, but also adjacent
L236@P4: cells. This receptor then may be a sensitive environmental reporter that reverses signal flow by enabling proximal endothelial cells to respond to activated PMN.
L237@P4: Soluble IL-6Ra may be a particularly relevant proinflammatory mediator following bacterial invasion. PMN exposed
L238@P4: to the bacterial product FMLP (above), or monocytes exposed
L239@P4: to pore-forming exotoxins (32) or bacterially derived metalloproteinases (33) shed their IL-6 receptor. Also, circulating
L240@P4: sIL-6Ra increases during sepsis (34), HIV infection (35), and
L241@P4: reperfusion injury (36), although a part of this is due to mRNA
L242@P4: alternative splicing (37). Recent data show the influx of PMN
L243@P4: into inflamed joints correlates with the increased concentration of sIL-6Ra in synovial fluid (38), and that sIL-6Ra can act
L244@P4: as a paracrine mediator localized to its site of generation (39).
